evidence.note: Skepticism about Shkval speed claims and greater confidence in Spearfish data shape the preference between the weapons.
Shkval's limited maneuvering and deployment are weighed against Spearfish's ability to maneuver and attack.

segments.summary: The preference for Spearfish rests on confidence in its performance data and maneuvering ability, while Shkval's claimed speed and practical value remain disputed.
segments.question: Is the VA-111 Shkval a faster torpedo than Spearfish?
segments.answerShort: The claimed Shkval figures are treated with skepticism. Spearfish is preferred for its more trusted data and its ability to maneuver during an attack.

segments.title: Was Shkval intended for a defensive snapshot?
segments.body: A viewer proposes firing Shkval rapidly along the bearing of an incoming torpedo to force the attacker to maneuver and disrupt its attack. The suggestion includes a possible nuclear warhead. It is accepted as one discussed operating concept, without establishing that it was the weapon's only purpose.

evidence.note: A viewer's proposed defensive snapshot receives qualified confirmation as one concept of operation for Shkval.

segments.summary: A viewer's proposed defensive snapshot receives qualified confirmation as one concept of operation for Shkval.
segments.question: Was Shkval intended for a rapid, possibly nuclear-tipped defensive shot along the bearing of an incoming torpedo?
segments.answerShort: That was broadly one of the operating concepts discussed for it.

segments.title: What was wrong with Tigerfish?
segments.body: Tigerfish's early reliability receives a strongly negative assessment, including an unfavorable comparison with the Mark 14. British recognition of the problems and subsequent improvement qualify that criticism.

evidence.note: The criticism concerns Tigerfish's early unreliability, with later improvement explicitly acknowledged.

segments.summary: The criticism concerns Tigerfish's early unreliability, with later improvement explicitly acknowledged.
segments.question: What was wrong with Tigerfish?
segments.answerShort: Its initial reliability was very poor, although the British acknowledged the faults and improved it.

segments.title: Alfa-class speed collided with Soviet personnel structure
segments.body: The Alfa class demanded technical skills that Soviet conscript personnel could not readily provide, so the boats operated with all-officer crews. Some of the best graduates then performed work normally assigned to junior sailors, gaining little experience of leading people before moving to other boats. A comparable Western vessel is imagined with experienced chiefs and senior officers, rather than junior personnel. These personnel problems coexisted with a formidable hunter-killer role: Alfas would wait for NATO submarines attempting to reach Soviet ballistic-missile boats while other Soviet submarines pushed beyond NATO barriers. The wider comparison stresses how professional NCOs preserved institutional knowledge and trained successive groups of conscripts. Soviet efforts to establish a comparable corps are judged unsuccessful here.

evidence.note: Technical requirements and conscript limitations led to all-officer crews, with junior officers gaining little leadership experience before later postings.
The all-officer arrangement is compared with a hypothetical Western crew of experienced chiefs and senior officers, with aviation examples qualifying the comparison.
Alfas are assigned a hunter-killer role against NATO submarines approaching Soviet ballistic-missile boats.
Professional NCOs preserved institutional knowledge in Western conscript forces, while Soviet attempts to build a comparable corps are judged unsuccessful.

segments.summary: The Alfa class combined a formidable hunter-killer role with an all-officer crewing model that revealed the Soviet Navy's weak professional enlisted and NCO structure.

segments.title: Kiev and the Yak-38 solved a peacetime air-cover problem
segments.body: The Kiev class extended the Moskvas' anti-submarine role and carried Yak-38 fighters for a limited peacetime mission. NATO reconnaissance aircraft could approach Soviet exercises far from land, where radio threats offered little control and shooting down an aircraft risked war. A carrier fighter could intercept the intruder and try to drive it away, giving the task group another way to respond. The Yak-38 is judged adequate for this role despite poor prospects against serious carrier fighters.

evidence.note: Initial uncertainty over Kiev's construction, its improved anti-submarine role, and its Yak-38 aircraft.
An aircraft interception offered an alternative to ineffective radio threats or shooting down an observer.
The Yak-38's peacetime usefulness is distinguished from its poor expected performance against serious carrier fighters.

segments.summary: Kiev's Yak-38 fighters could challenge reconnaissance aircraft around distant Soviet exercises, providing a response between radio warnings and opening fire.

segments.title: Why did the Sea Harrier have better fighter prospects than the Yak-38?
segments.body: The Sea Harrier Mark II had beyond-visual-range capability and effective missiles, giving it a chance against more capable opponents. That equipment is the reason offered for treating a Harrier engagement differently from sending up a Yak-38. The judgment is more cautious for first-generation Sea Harriers against the Soviet fighters named in the question.

evidence.note: Beyond-visual-range weapons gave the later Sea Harrier a chance that the Yak-38 lacked.

segments.summary: Beyond-visual-range weapons gave the later Sea Harrier a chance that the Yak-38 lacked.
segments.question: Was taking a Yak-38 against a powerful fighter any worse than taking a Harrier against a MiG-29 or Su-27?
segments.answerShort: Yes in this comparison: the later Sea Harrier had beyond-visual-range weapons and good missiles, while the assessment of first-generation Sea Harriers is more cautious.

segments.title: Kirovs served as capital ships and differed from hull to hull
segments.body: The Kirovs are classified as capital ships in this interpretation because of their scale and intended global presence role. They joined several other Soviet ship types equipped to command dispersed task groups. Construction took long enough that successive hulls differed visibly rather than emerging to one identical standard. They remained a related class, but each ship reflected a prolonged individual building process.

evidence.note: Global status, presence, and task-group command functions across several Soviet ship types.
Long individual construction periods and visible differences between successive Kirovs.

segments.summary: The Kirovs' presence and command roles support a capital-ship interpretation, while their long construction periods explain differences between individual ships.

segments.title: A surviving Soviet Union might have revived US strike cruisers
segments.body: A longer-lived Soviet Union is the premise for a possible American response to the Kirovs. The suggestion is that US strike cruisers, or a comparable large nuclear cruiser, might then have been built. Older American nuclear surface ships were approaching replacement, creating another reason to consider such a project. This remains a counterfactual judgment about procurement.

evidence.note: The possible revival of a large US nuclear cruiser depends on the counterfactual continuation of the Soviet Union.

segments.summary: The possible revival of a large US nuclear cruiser depends on the counterfactual continuation of the Soviet Union.

segments.title: Hospital ships could answer Soviet prestige only where aid was welcome
segments.body: A viewer, Paul, proposes hospital and construction ships as a response to a Kirov's visit. A smaller warship could look unimpressive, while a carrier group could make the Soviet ship appear to require an excessive response. Humanitarian assistance offers a different diplomatic purpose. Its reception still depends on the government concerned: aid welcomed after a disaster or by a small island state could look patronizing in a country with substantial hospitals of its own.

evidence.note: A hospital-ship visit could offer useful assistance after a Soviet warship visit, but an unwanted offer could embarrass the receiving government.

segments.summary: A hospital-ship visit could offer useful assistance after a Soviet warship visit, but an unwanted offer could embarrass the receiving government.

segments.title: Did cost alone explain the move away from nuclear cruisers?
segments.body: A cost objection to nuclear cruisers is accepted. The end of the Soviet Union is added as a factor that made the decision easier, because the principal naval opponent no longer had to be faced.

evidence.note: Nuclear-cruiser costs are considered alongside the changed threat after the Soviet collapse.

segments.summary: Nuclear-cruiser costs are considered alongside the changed threat after the Soviet collapse.
segments.question: Were nuclear cruisers too expensive to be worthwhile compared with gas-turbine ships?
segments.answerShort: The cost concern is accepted, with the qualification that the Soviet collapse made the decision easier.

segments.title: Typhoon and Delta reveal parallel Soviet SSBN priorities
segments.body: The Typhoon did not simply replace one exhausted ballistic-missile submarine line. Successive Yankee and Delta programs overlapped, and Delta IV construction continued after the Typhoon run ended. Breaking through ice and carrying a large missile provide operational explanations, but they leave the question of why the Soviet Navy wanted simultaneous programs. The interpretation offered here assigns an additional role to the status of possessing the world's largest submarine. Claims that the missile was simply a response to Trident are also challenged through the long development process and the difference between initial operational capability and a mature system.

evidence.note: Overlapping Yankee and Delta programs, followed by Typhoon construction alongside Delta variants.
Status is proposed as a reason for retaining the enormous Typhoon alongside the Delta IV.
Long development times and early service declarations complicate comparisons based on introduction dates.

segments.summary: The continued Delta IV program alongside the enormous Typhoon suggests that survivability and missile requirements operated together with the political value of possessing the world's largest submarine.

segments.title: Slava cruisers filled gaps beneath the Kirovs
segments.body: The Slavas filled several gaps as older Soviet cruisers left service. They provided a second option if the Kirovs failed and offered stronger air defence on paper than many existing cruisers. Their missiles were useful even though newer systems were available. A comparison with British Crown Colony cruisers explains the appeal of a ship adequate for its jobs without building the largest alternative. Yard problems, difficulty obtaining systems, and the project's lower priority frustrated that expectation and limited the completed force to three ships.

evidence.note: Backfilling cruiser roles, insurance against Kirov failure, and improved air defence on paper.
Crown Colony analogy and delays caused by yard problems, system supply, and low project priority.

segments.summary: Slava cruisers offered a practical second tier of missile and air-defence capability, but yard and supply problems prevented easy production.

segments.title: Can a Typhoon launch ballistic missiles from the pier?
segments.body: The Typhoon's missile range allowed a theoretical launch from alongside at Murmansk. The objection concerns readiness: if a crisis had reached the point of possible nuclear launch, deployable submarines should already be at sea. A boat alongside for maintenance might also have had its missiles removed, because the weapons needed servicing too. The ability to launch from port therefore does not establish that a particular submarine would be armed and ready there.

evidence.note: Theoretical launch from Murmansk, the expectation of prior deployment in a crisis, and missile removal during maintenance.

segments.summary: A theoretical launch from Murmansk raises separate questions about warning, deployment, and whether a submarine in maintenance still carries missiles.
segments.question: Could a Typhoon-class submarine launch its ballistic missiles while alongside at Murmansk?
segments.answerShort: In principle, yes. The criticism is that a deployable boat needed in a nuclear crisis should already be at sea, while one in maintenance might have its missiles removed.

segments.title: Were ballistic missiles considered for surface ships?
segments.body: Surface ships were considered as ballistic-missile platforms. Italian cruiser proposals are recalled tentatively, while the reasons the wider concept was not adopted remain unexplained.

evidence.note: Italian cruiser proposals illustrate that ballistic missiles were considered for surface ships.

segments.summary: Italian cruiser proposals illustrate that ballistic missiles were considered for surface ships.
segments.question: Were surface ships considered as launch platforms for ballistic missiles?
segments.answerShort: Yes. Italian cruiser proposals and other surface-ship ideas are recalled, with their abandonment left unexplained.

segments.title: Which part of the Soviet nuclear triad was most capable?
segments.body: Land-based ballistic missiles receive a tentative preference. The Soviet nuclear triad as a whole is still judged capable and dangerous. The existence of counters to each part does not by itself make the force ineffective.

evidence.note: Land-based missiles receive a tentative preference, with a qualification that all parts of the Soviet triad remained capable.

segments.summary: Land-based missiles receive a tentative preference, with a qualification that all parts of the Soviet triad remained capable.
segments.question: What was the most capable part of the Soviet nuclear triad?
segments.answerShort: Probably the land-based ballistic missiles, with the qualification that the whole triad remained capable.

segments.title: Did fear of another Barbarossa justify launching from port?
segments.body: A viewer suggests that fear of a surprise attack explains the value of launching missiles from alongside. The response distinguishes the Soviet Navy's memory of Barbarossa from Stalin's surprise. Kuznetsov had recognized the danger, placed the fleet on alert, and sent deployable ships to sea. In this argument, that precedent supports timely deployment rather than dependence on a launch from port.

evidence.note: Kuznetsov's wartime alert is used to challenge a surprise-attack argument for keeping a retaliatory launch option alongside.

segments.summary: Kuznetsov's wartime alert is used to challenge a surprise-attack argument for keeping a retaliatory launch option alongside.
segments.question: Did Soviet fear of a surprise attack like Barbarossa make pier-side launch capability useful?
segments.answerShort: The response argues that Kuznetsov had anticipated Barbarossa and deployed available ships, so the navy's own precedent favored acting on warning.

segments.title: Why did Soviet carriers also carry cruiser-style missiles?
segments.body: The quality and capabilities of the embarked aircraft are offered as the explanation for combining aviation with cruiser-style missile armament. The carrier's weapons therefore need to be considered alongside what its aircraft could do.

evidence.note: Aircraft capability is offered as a reason for Soviet carriers' substantial missile armament.

segments.summary: Aircraft capability is offered as a reason for Soviet carriers' substantial missile armament.
segments.question: Was there a logical reason Soviet carriers also functioned as missile cruisers?
segments.answerShort: The explanation offered is the quality and capabilities of the aircraft fitted to them.

segments.title: How is the Soviet reaction to Able Archer 83 interpreted?
segments.body: A viewer cites the Soviet reaction to Able Archer 83 as a challenge to the argument about surprise attacks. The reply interprets part of that reaction as staged for political purposes. The claim concerns part of the reaction and remains an interpretation.

evidence.note: Part of the Soviet reaction to Able Archer 83 is interpreted as politically staged.

segments.summary: Part of the Soviet reaction to Able Archer 83 is interpreted as politically staged.
segments.question: How does the Soviet reaction to Able Archer 83 affect the argument about surprise attacks?
segments.answerShort: The reply argues that part of the reaction was staged for political purposes.

segments.title: Kuznetsov combined short takeoff with arrested recovery
segments.body: Kuznetsov appeared to open a more credible carrier phase for the Soviet Navy. Its aircraft took off under their own power, as on the smaller carrier types used for comparison. Recovery used arresting equipment. The combination allowed a heavier landing than relying on vertical recovery and explains the practical distinction behind STOBAR.

evidence.note: The carrier's short-takeoff and arrested-recovery arrangement and the resulting recovery-weight distinction.

segments.summary: Kuznetsov's STOBAR arrangement combined aircraft-powered takeoff with arrested recovery and a higher recovery weight.

segments.title: When does ballistic-missile accuracy change the target set?
segments.body: A viewer challenges the claim that landing within 10 rather than 100 metres makes little difference, pointing to hardened structures. The objection is accepted, alongside a correction of an earlier recollection of megaton yields. The distinction then turns to mission: the retaliatory submarine weapons considered here are treated as weapons aimed at cities, while accurate land-based missiles are associated with hardened targets. This is an account of their assigned roles, rather than a claim that every submarine missile has the same targeting limits. Payload figures also need care because some positions can carry decoys to draw defences away from warheads.

evidence.note: A viewer's hardened-target objection is accepted, the earlier yield recollection is corrected, and Soviet retaliatory submarine weapons are characterized as targeting cities.
The role distinction associates primary-strike land-based missiles with hardened targets and retaliatory submarine weapons with unhardened targets.
Decoys can occupy payload positions to divert attention from nuclear warheads.

segments.summary: The importance of accuracy depends on the target and assigned mission, with a viewer's hardened-target objection prompting a qualification and a correction of the earlier yield estimate.
segments.question: Would a warhead landing within 10 meters rather than 100 meters matter?
segments.answerShort: Yes against hardened targets, but the retaliatory submarine-launched weapons discussed here were aimed at softer urban targets, where that difference mattered less.

segments.title: Pier-side launch raises a personal objection about hull damage
segments.body: A personal naval-architecture objection concerns the possibility that a surfaced missile launch could damage the submarine's hull, unlike a launch after submerging. A viewer counters that future maintenance would matter little once a nuclear exchange had begun. That counterargument is accepted as probably removing the practical concern, while discomfort at deliberately damaging a submarine remains. The conceded last-resort circumstances qualify the objection about damage.

evidence.note: A concern about launch damage to a surfaced hull, contrasted with submerging before firing.
Personal engineering discomfort persists after accepting that maintenance is probably not a practical concern once nuclear missiles are being launched.

segments.summary: Concern about damage from a surfaced launch is qualified by acceptance that preserving the boat may no longer matter in a nuclear exchange.

segments.title: Could a Zumwalt answer a Russian cruiser's presence?
segments.body: The suggested response is a Zumwalt visiting after a Russian cruiser. Its suitability is qualified by the damage to its public reputation, which is judged to weaken its value in an exercise about prestige.

evidence.note: A ship's public reputation can affect the diplomatic value of sending it to answer a rival's visit.

segments.summary: A ship's public reputation can affect the diplomatic value of sending it to answer a rival's visit.
segments.question: Would sending a Zumwalt be enough to answer a Russian cruiser visit?
segments.answerShort: It is judged potentially sufficient, with the qualification that its damaged public reputation would weaken that response.

segments.title: Did Typhoons deploy cruise missiles through their torpedo tubes?
segments.body: Cruise missiles launched through 650 mm torpedo tubes are acknowledged as a possible Typhoon load. Whether boats actually deployed with that load remains uncertain. The distinction is between a proposed capability and confirmed operational carriage.

evidence.note: A possible Typhoon cruise-missile load is distinguished from uncertainty over actual deployment.

segments.summary: A possible Typhoon cruise-missile load is distinguished from uncertainty over actual deployment.
segments.question: Did Typhoons carry first-strike cruise missiles for their 650 mm torpedo tubes?
segments.answerShort: They could theoretically have carried that load, but actual deployment is left unconfirmed.

segments.title: Kuznetsov's problems are linked to its builders despite earlier carrier experience
segments.body: Kuznetsov followed several earlier Soviet aviation ships, so a complete lack of carrier experience is rejected as an explanation for its problems. The emphasis falls on the Black Sea shipyard and the wider group of yards also struggling with Slava construction. The same builders were intended to produce Ulyanovsk, a nuclear carrier combining catapults with a ski-jump arrangement. That mixture complicates the idea that it was simply a copy of an American carrier. Earlier successful cruiser construction is contrasted with the difficulties associated with later large ships.

evidence.note: Earlier aviation-ship construction and the argument that Kuznetsov's problems lay with the builders.
Ulyanovsk's planned nuclear propulsion and mixed launch arrangements, followed by criticism of the yard's later construction record.

segments.summary: The Soviet Navy had earlier carrier experience; Kuznetsov's difficulties are instead associated with its shipyard and the construction of increasingly demanding ships.

segments.title: What could Soviet carriers do short of peer war?
segments.body: In a regional conflict, a Soviet carrier could provide airstrikes and air support to allied forces. Civil wars in Africa supply the example. The deployment would also demonstrate power and support for the ally's government. This interpretation gives carriers a political and military role short of fighting American carrier groups.

evidence.note: Carrier airstrikes and air support for allied forces in civil wars, with a visible power-projection role.

segments.summary: Carrier air support could help allies in regional conflicts and demonstrate Soviet commitment.
segments.question: What would the Soviet Union use aircraft carriers for in a non-peer or near-peer conflict?
segments.answerShort: They could support allies in regional conflicts with airstrikes and visible power projection, especially in Africa and other contested regions.

segments.title: How did a low-priority Soviet Navy secure major projects?
segments.body: The navy's position behind the strategic forces, army, and air force is accepted with qualifications. Gorshkov nevertheless secured substantial funding for major naval projects. His ability to work around political obstacles is offered as the explanation for why formal priority did not determine every procurement outcome.

evidence.note: Gorshkov's political ability helped major naval projects obtain funding despite the service's lower place among competing priorities.

segments.summary: Gorshkov's political ability helped major naval projects obtain funding despite the service's lower place among competing priorities.
segments.question: Was the Soviet Navy fourth in line behind the strategic forces, army, and air force?
segments.answerShort: To an extent, yes, but Gorshkov still secured substantial funding for major naval projects.

segments.title: Chernavin continued major programs after Gorshkov
segments.body: Vladimir Chernavin succeeded Gorshkov after a long period of preparation under him. He commanded the Soviet Navy from 1985 to 1991 and then briefly the Commonwealth of Independent States Navy. The transition preserved the Akula program and other existing projects. The principal change described is the stopping of some newer projects.

evidence.note: Chernavin's succession preserved established programs after Gorshkov's long command.

segments.summary: Chernavin's succession preserved established programs after Gorshkov's long command.

segments.title: Ulyanovsk's proposed air group was overtaken by cancellation
segments.body: Ulyanovsk was canceled while incomplete, at roughly forty percent completion in this account, with scrapping following in February 1992. Its proposed air group included Yak-44 radar-picket aircraft. Su-33 and MiG-29K fighters were considered for the fighter complement. A mixed force of about 44 fighters is recalled, while the precise composition remains open to debate.

evidence.note: The incomplete carrier was intended to carry fixed-wing early warning and a fighter force whose exact composition remained disputed.

segments.summary: The incomplete carrier was intended to carry fixed-wing early warning and a fighter force whose exact composition remained disputed.

segments.title: Would Ulyanovsk have retained heavy missiles?
segments.body: Ulyanovsk was still intended to carry twelve P-700 Granit surface-to-surface missiles. Surface-to-air missiles and other defensive systems also remained in the design. Enlarging the carrier air capability therefore did not mean abandoning substantial missile armament.

evidence.note: Ulyanovsk retained twelve P-700 Granit missiles in addition to air-defence systems.

segments.summary: Ulyanovsk retained twelve P-700 Granit missiles in addition to air-defence systems.
segments.question: Did Ulyanovsk give up the heavy missile armament of earlier Soviet carriers?
segments.answerShort: No. The planned armament still included twelve P-700 Granit missiles and air-defence systems.

segments.title: The late Soviet fleet struggled to fill its middle tier
segments.body: The Soviet Navy repeatedly struggled to provide the medium ships between its largest combatants and smaller vessels. High and low capability mean different things in different threat environments. In the World War II comparison, sloops occupy the low end of a low-threat setting, while destroyers and cruisers occupy intermediate positions and capital ships sit at the high end of a dangerous one. The middle ship must serve as the stronger vessel in routine operations and the lesser unit in a major force. The mix therefore concerns efficient operational use as well as cost. Danish use of interchangeable StanFlex components provides a brief example of using common ships for different tasks.

evidence.note: A frigate program prompts an explanation of the medium-ship gap and how high and low capability change with the threat environment.
Operational efficiency as well as cost, followed by the Danish example of ships using interchangeable StanFlex components.

segments.summary: The middle tier links routine presence to high-threat operations, so a fleet's high-low mix depends on mission as well as cost.

segments.title: Would airborne early warning have helped in the Falklands?
segments.body: The Royal Navy would have welcomed Hawkeyes or Gannets if a suitable carrier had been available to operate them. Helicopter airborne early warning is also treated as a capability that would have been valuable during the fighting. Those helicopters arrived after the war, with Illustrious recalled as the carrier bringing them south.

evidence.note: Fixed-wing or helicopter airborne early warning would have been welcome during the Falklands fighting, but the helicopter capability arrived afterward.

segments.summary: Fixed-wing or helicopter airborne early warning would have been welcome during the Falklands fighting, but the helicopter capability arrived afterward.
segments.question: Would the Royal Navy have welcomed Hawkeyes during the Falklands War if it had a carrier able to launch them?
segments.answerShort: Yes, and Gannets or the helicopter early-warning capability that arrived after the war would also have been welcome.

segments.title: Gorshkov's long command depended on managing political support
segments.body: Gorshkov supplied a continuing influence through nearly thirty years of Soviet naval leadership, spanning entire service careers. Other officers and institutions still mattered, so the fleet's history cannot be reduced to one person. The industrial system could deliver what factories produced rather than exactly what the armed forces requested. Political priorities shaped both sides of that relationship. Gorshkov is credited with judging which disputes would end in his favor and letting other people spend political capital arguing for outcomes he wanted.

evidence.note: Nearly thirty years of leadership provided continuity across entire naval careers, alongside other people and institutions.
Industry's influence over deliveries is qualified by the argument that Soviet political priorities came first.
Gorshkov is credited with allowing others to expend political capital on outcomes he favored.

segments.summary: Nearly thirty years in command allowed Gorshkov to guide procurement through a system in which political priorities shaped industry and military requirements.

segments.title: Completing Stalingrad could have affected Vanguard's retirement
segments.body: Stalin's desire for capital ships faced industrial and yard limitations even at the height of his authority. A counterfactual extends his life long enough for Stalingrad to launch and potentially enter service. A battlecruiser carrying his name would then have been politically difficult to remove. Its existence could also have encouraged Britain to retain Vanguard in reserve beyond 1960, despite the cost, to avoid appearing to fall below Soviet naval status.

evidence.note: A hypothetical completed Stalingrad links Soviet prestige to the possible continued retention of HMS Vanguard.

segments.summary: A hypothetical completed Stalingrad links Soviet prestige to the possible continued retention of HMS Vanguard.

segments.title: Larger missiles could help justify larger Soviet ships
segments.body: A hypothetical procurement sequence begins with the navy asking for a missile no larger than its predecessor. Engineers instead present political leaders with a bigger and better weapon, a proposal with greater prestige. Its added weight and length then force changes to the ship intended to carry it. The navy can use those requirements to justify a larger hull and more funding while competing with the army and air force. The example explains how political incentives could turn an unwanted increase in weapon size into support for naval construction.

evidence.note: A hypothetical missile program shows how weapon growth could become the political justification for a larger ship.

segments.summary: A hypothetical missile program shows how weapon growth could become the political justification for a larger ship.

segments.title: Why retain old Russian ships for so long?
segments.body: Decommissioning ships could make the navy appear weaker. Preserving the appearance of strength is the political explanation offered for keeping them.

evidence.note: The political cost of appearing weaker is offered as a reason to retain old ships.

segments.summary: The political cost of appearing weaker is offered as a reason to retain old ships.
segments.question: Why did Russia keep ships around for so long?
segments.answerShort: Because decommissioning them could make it look weak.
